summary: Belgium is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (ETIAS is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa applied for through a Belgian embassy or visa center.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

tips.text: Canada's travel advice says pickpockets target passengers on the metro, at airports and at train stations, and that petty crime is frequent at Brussels-Nord, Brussels-Central and Brussels-Midi stations and on Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam and Brussels–London trains.
The 90-day visa-free limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Belgium — days spent in France or the Netherlands draw on the same allowance.
Belgium's official languages are Dutch, French and German, per the EU's country page.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Belgium?
faq.answer: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa from a Belgian embassy or visa center.

faq.question: How much does a Belgium Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: €90 for adults, €45 for children aged 6–11 and free for under-6s. The fee is set EU-wide. Applications go through the Belgian mission or visa center serving your place of residence.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Belgium?
faq.answer: ETIAS is the EU's travel authorization for visa-exempt visitors. It is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Once mandatory, it will cost €20 (free for under-18s and over-70s) and be valid for 3 years.

faq.question: How do I stay in Belgium longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: You need a long-stay (type D) visa or residence permit tied to a purpose such as work, study or family reunification, applied for at the Belgian mission before travel.

faq.question: Can EU citizens enter Belgium with just an ID card?
faq.answer: Yes — EU, EEA and Swiss citizens can enter with a valid national identity card instead of a passport, and can stay without a visa.
